articles.title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
articles.text:
237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
- Date:
- November 10, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Davis
- Summary:
- A bizarre, heavily armored amphibian roamed the oceans 237 million years ago, despite the fact that modern amphibians cannot survive entirely in saltwater. Discovered in China, the giant salamander-sized creature may be the first known amphibian to have adapted to a fully marine existence.
- Share:
A remarkable fossil discovery in China has revealed an ancient amphibian that lived entirely in the ocean, something no amphibian alive today is known to do. The unusual animal, named Gerrothorax maritimus, had a broad, flattened body protected by bony armor and was roughly the size of a giant salamander. Researchers believe it spent much of its life on the seafloor, waiting to ambush passing prey.
The discovery comes from an international team at the University of California, Davis, Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. Their findings, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, are based on two exceptionally well-preserved skeletons dating back nearly 237 million years to the Late Triassic period.
Both fossils were uncovered in China's Guizhou Province, in a region that was once submerged beneath an ancient ocean hundreds of miles from major landmasses.
"This area is part of an ecosystem that we've been looking at and trying to reconstruct," said study corresponding author Ryosuke Motani, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at UC Davis. "We've been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian, and it's a sort of very unusual member of the lineage."
The finding is especially surprising because amphibians are generally unable to survive in seawater. Among the more than 8,000 amphibian species living today, none are known to spend their entire lives in marine environments, and fewer than 2% have any ability to tolerate salt.
Mammals, reptiles, and birds, by comparison, all include species that can live entirely at sea without relying on land for food or fresh water. Until this discovery, scientists had never identified convincing fossil evidence of an amphibian with the same ability.
A Giant Armored Amphibian Built for the Seafloor
Because the two skeletons are so complete, researchers were able to piece together the animal's appearance and develop a clearer picture of how it lived.
Gerrothorax maritimus measured nearly three feet long, but its proportions were far different from those of a modern salamander. Rather than having a long, slender body, it was unusually broad and flattened, with a distinctive disc-shaped form.
Its body was also covered in thick bony armor, which may have helped protect it from large marine predators such as ichthyosaurs.
"If you think about today's amphibians, this animal is unusual because it's big," Motani said. "It's probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what's different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky."
The structure of its skull, together with its heavy armor, suggests that this ancient amphibian was an ambush predator. Instead of actively chasing its meals, it likely rested on the seafloor until an unsuspecting animal came within reach.
"They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in," said Motani, who noted that the hunting strategy resembles that of the wobbegong, a type of carpet shark that lives near the seafloor and captures prey using suction.
How Could an Amphibian Survive in Salt Water?
One of the biggest mysteries surrounding Gerrothorax maritimus is how it managed to survive in an environment that is hostile to nearly all modern amphibians.
The problem comes down largely to amphibian skin. Unlike the relatively waterproof skin of many other animals, amphibian skin allows water and gases to pass through it. This makes it useful for breathing and maintaining hydration, but also leaves amphibians especially vulnerable to the effects of salt water.
"That skin is permeable, and that allows the animals to use it for multiple purposes," said Motani. "They use it for respiration and water intake, so amphibians don't drink or breathe through the mouth because they can do both through the skin."
As a result, modern amphibians generally depend on freshwater habitats or environments close to them. A few species have developed limited salt tolerance, including the crab-eating frog. Even these animals can lose weight when exposed to brackish water and must eventually return to freshwater to recover.
The ancient Gerrothorax maritimus, however, may have evolved a very different solution.
Researchers suggest that its extensive bony armor restricted the movement of water through its skin. This protective covering may have reduced its dependence on absorbing water directly through the skin, allowing the animal to take in seawater through its mouth instead.
Under this proposed mechanism, water would have been absorbed through the digestive tract, while the animal's gills could have helped eliminate excess salt. Gills are known to have been present in members of the Gerrothorax genus, giving the researchers reason to suspect that this species possessed a more fishlike approach to managing its salt balance.
Together, these adaptations may explain how an amphibian managed to occupy an ecological niche that remains inaccessible to its modern relatives.
Fossil Evidence Points to a Fully Marine Lifestyle
The researchers also examined whether Gerrothorax maritimus truly lived in the ocean or whether its remains might have been transported there after death.
Several clues strongly favor a marine lifestyle.
First, the skeletons were recovered from sediments deposited in a deep marine environment. Their remarkable completeness also provides important evidence about where the animals died.
"Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom," said Motani. "But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived."
The preservation of such delicate skeletal structures suggests that the bodies were not carried long distances before reaching the seafloor.
To investigate further, the team analyzed the fossils' chemical composition, focusing on the relative abundance of different forms of strontium, known as isotopes.
The results closely matched the strontium isotope signatures expected in ocean water during the Late Triassic, providing another independent line of evidence that the animals inhabited a marine environment.
Taken together, the fossil preservation, geological setting, and chemical findings make a compelling case that Gerrothorax maritimus spent its life entirely at sea.
The discovery reveals an unexpected evolutionary path for amphibians, showing that at least one ancient species appears to have overcome the biological limitations that keep its living relatives largely confined to freshwater environments.
The research received funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

articles.title: Suni Williams rides through NYC during Vets Day Parade | Space photo of the day for Nov. 13, 2026
articles.text:
Astronaut Suni Williams rides through NYC as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade | Space photo of the day for Nov. 13, 2026
Navy veteran Suni Williams leads in a longstanding astronaut tradition.
New Yorkers got a space-y surprise on Wednesday (Nov. 11): Retired NASA astronaut and U.S. Navy Captain Sunita "Suni" Williams rolled down 5th Avenue in the back of a classic convertible wrapped in patriotic decals as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade.
What is it?
On Wednesday, New York City's 107th annual Veterans Day Parade made its way through Manhattan to the cheers and respectful nods of thousands of onlookers.
The parade is an annual tradition on the holiday, which honors veterans of the U.S. armed forces. As part of the parade, veterans, active-duty soldiers, firefighters, marching bands, youth cadets and more march through the city and honor those who have served and sacrificed in the U.S. military.
This year, the parade featured Suni Williams as its grand marshal. "I’m proud to join New Yorkers and Americans from around the country in honoring the service, sacrifice, and commitment of veterans from every generation," she said during the event.
Why is it incredible?
Williams was selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1998 and retired from it in December 2025. She spent 608 days in space during her astronaut career, the second-most by an American astronaut behind Peggy Whitson, who racked up 695.
Williams also had an extensive career in the U.S. Navy. She began as an ensign in 1987 before serving in a number of different roles. For example, she was a diving officer and a naval aviator and also provided helicopter combat support during Operation Desert Shield and Operation Provide Comfort. She further served as a squadron safety officer and finally as a captain, a rank she achieved in 2017.
During this time, Williams supported relief efforts following Hurricane Andrew, trained within the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School and gained a wealth of further experience flying as a military pilot.
Williams is part of a longstanding tradition of astronauts serving in the U.S. military. From test pilots to naval officers and more, there's a strong link between the U.S. armed forces and NASA's astronaut program.
Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music

articles.title: Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images
articles.text:
Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images
- Date:
- November 10, 2026
- Source:
- California Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- A breakthrough in telescope imaging could reveal countless alien worlds that have been hiding in plain sight. Scientists developed a new technique that uses a digital twin of the James Webb Space Telescope to remove the overwhelming glare of stars, making faint exoplanets two to 15 times easier to detect than with conventional methods. The technology has already uncovered a previously hidden planet in existing telescope data and could reveal many more.
- Share:
The Milky Way is believed to contain billions of planets beyond our solar system. These distant worlds, known as exoplanets, offer astronomers an opportunity to explore other planetary systems, identify potentially habitable environments, and perhaps eventually discover evidence of life elsewhere in the universe.
Finding these planets is one challenge. Actually seeing them is another. Most exoplanets orbit stars that shine so brightly that the planets become nearly impossible to distinguish from the surrounding glare. Even the most advanced space telescopes struggle to separate the faint light of a distant planet from the overwhelming brightness of its host star.
Now, researchers have developed a powerful new method for removing that starlight from telescope images, revealing planets that were previously hidden. The technique uses a sophisticated computer simulation of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and has already exposed an exoplanet that was concealed in existing observations. In tests involving known planets, it achieved two to 15 times greater detection sensitivity than conventional approaches.
A Digital Twin of James Webb Reveals Hidden Planets
The breakthrough centers on a virtual replica of Webb's Near Infrared Camera (NIRCam), an instrument designed to observe the universe in infrared light. By recreating how the camera operates, researchers can identify and correct tiny imperfections that interfere with its observations.
The virtual model, often called a "digital twin," allows scientists to simulate the telescope's behavior and determine how starlight spreads through its optical system. Once they understand the patterns produced by the star, they can digitally subtract much of that glare, making faint planets easier to detect.
"Directly imaging exoplanets is incredibly challenging because even the tiniest imperfections in a telescope can make it difficult to separate the faint light of a planet from the overwhelming glare of its star," explains Caltech's Katie Bouman, professor of computing and mathematical sciences, electrical engineering and astronomy, a Rosenberg Scholar, and a Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator, who is a co-author of a Nature paper about the new method published online November 4.
"What's exciting is that we're showing how computation can help overcome limitations of the telescope itself," Bouman continues. "By combining a physical model of the instrument with optimization techniques from machine learning, we have been able to remove starlight much more precisely, making it easier to detect faint exoplanets and even reveal one that was previously hidden in the JWST data."
How Scientists Make Blinding Starlight Disappear
The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP). Rather than relying entirely on improvements to telescope hardware, the system uses advanced computation to correct problems in images that have already been collected.
To develop FLIP, the team created a detailed physical model of Webb's infrared camera. They then used computational techniques to examine millions of possible imperfections, subtle changes, and other unknown factors that could influence the telescope's observations.
These small variations matter because even an extremely slight distortion can alter how a star appears in an image. When astronomers attempt to remove the star's light, any remaining glare can overwhelm the much dimmer signal from a nearby planet.
By accounting for these effects, FLIP produces a highly precise model of the star's appearance. Researchers can then subtract that modeled starlight from the original observations, allowing previously obscured objects to become visible.
"This is the first time that we have demonstrated that these little imperfections or instabilities are not a limiting factor in the kinds of planets we can image," says lead author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, a graduate student at Northwestern University in the lab of astronomer Jason Wang, who is also a co-author of the paper. "As you go through this iterative process of trying to find what the telescope actually is doing during observations, you basically see the glare of the star disappearing in very bizarre ways. It gets dimmer and very deformed until at the end you get a pretty clean image and, if you're lucky, there's a blob there, which is a glowing planet."
A Failed Experiment Led to a Major Breakthrough
The idea behind FLIP began taking shape when Ferrer-Chavez was an undergraduate student at the Autonomous University of Yucatán in Mexico. He had already participated in a Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship project with Wang, who was then a 51 Pegasi b Postdoctoral Fellow (named after the first exoplanet discovered orbiting a Sun-like star) in the laboratory of Dimitri Mawet.
Mawet is the David Morrisroe Professor of Astronomy at Caltech and a senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is managed by Caltech. He also serves as director of instrumentation for the Caltech Optical Observatories.
At the time, Ferrer-Chavez was looking for additional opportunities to pursue research. Meanwhile, Wang had been discussing a potential collaboration with Bouman that would combine her expertise in computational imaging with his knowledge of astronomical instruments. Their shared goal was to improve the ability of telescopes to directly image exoplanets.
The two researchers brought Ferrer-Chavez into the project and began mentoring him. However, the initial effort did not produce the results they had hoped for.
"Rodrigo's senior thesis was an exploration of possible approaches, none of which ended up being what we did for this paper, but it helped rule out what not to do and also helped us understand the problem better," Wang says. "I believe our recent success was only possible because we did that exercise first."
Ferrer-Chavez originally attempted to train machine learning models to predict the patterns of starlight appearing in telescope data. That strategy proved unsuccessful, prompting the team to rethink how the technology could be used.
Instead of asking artificial intelligence to predict what the glare should look like, they turned to computational tools developed for machine learning to perform detailed physical calculations.
These methods allowed the researchers to adjust millions of variables, much like turning an enormous collection of control knobs. Each adjustment helped refine their simulation of the telescope until it more closely reproduced the actual observations. Performing this many calculations manually would be impractical.
The resulting approach combines the physical laws governing light and telescope optics with the computational power of modern optimization methods. Rather than simply guessing what should be removed from an image, FLIP uses a model of how the telescope produces that image in the first place.
James Webb's Archives May Contain More Hidden Worlds
One of the most exciting possibilities is that astronomers may not need new telescope observations to benefit from the discovery.
Webb has already collected enormous amounts of astronomical data, including images of stars that could harbor planets too faint to detect using earlier analysis methods. FLIP offers a way to revisit these observations and search for objects that were overlooked.
"We now have a tool that lets us discover and study planets that we were not able to 'see' before, even if that planet was already in an image in the JWST archive," Ferrer-Chavez explains. "We can try to find planets that may have been missed there, and also planets that perhaps we tried to image, but we could not actually detect at the time."
This means some planets that were previously considered beyond the reach of direct imaging could potentially be identified without sending another telescope into space.
It also changes how astronomers can think about existing observations. An image that appears to contain nothing but a brilliant star may hold additional information about planets hidden beneath its glare.
Pushing Telescopes Beyond Their Physical Limits
Astronomers have spent decades developing technology to reduce the overwhelming brightness of stars. One important tool is a coronagraph, an instrument designed to block starlight so that faint objects nearby can be observed more clearly.
For example, NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope carries a Coronagraph Instrument developed by researchers at Caltech, JPL, and IPAC (a science and data center for astronomy at Caltech). The instrument is specifically designed to suppress starlight and improve the direct imaging of exoplanets.
But even exceptionally precise telescope hardware has unavoidable limitations. Wang explains that physical instruments alone cannot match the level of correction achieved by FLIP when processing the images.
"The James Webb Space Telescope, which we demonstrated on, is optically stable to the nanometer level, which just sounds pretty awesome, but that's still limiting," he says. "We're excited because this technique is not limited specifically to JWST. Because of some very specific design, this technique could be used on any telescope."
A nanometer is one billionth of a meter, meaning Webb's optical system maintains extraordinary precision. Yet even disturbances on this incredibly small scale can interfere with the detection of planets next to bright stars.
FLIP offers a different way around that problem. Instead of requiring the telescope itself to eliminate every tiny imperfection, the technique mathematically accounts for those effects after the observations have been made.
The researchers now intend to refine FLIP and investigate how it could work with additional instruments, including the Roman Space Telescope and telescopes operating from Earth's surface.
A Powerful New Tool in the Search for Another Earth
The implications may extend well beyond today's observatories. The researchers believe their approach could help shape future space missions, particularly those designed to search for planets resembling Earth.
One major possibility is NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). The mission is intended to become the first telescope specifically designed to search for evidence of life on planets orbiting other stars.
A central objective would be to photograph Earth-like planets within the habitable zones of stars similar to our Sun. A habitable zone is the range of distances around a star where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on a planet's surface, assuming suitable atmospheric conditions.
But the technical challenge is enormous. An Earth-like planet orbiting a Sun-like star can be approximately 10 billion times fainter than the star itself, making the planet extraordinarily difficult to distinguish from the surrounding light.
"The goal of HWO is to find Earth-like planets and the habitable zones of Sun-like stars through a direct imaging method," Ferrer-Chavez says. "The engineering challenge of trying to image something that is around 10 billion times fainter than something right next to it is a brutal -- not just to clean the image but to build a telescope that can take that image."
FLIP could make that challenge more manageable. If astronomers can digitally remove more unwanted starlight after capturing an image, future telescope designs may not need to overcome every source of optical instability through hardware alone.
The approach could therefore give engineers greater flexibility while allowing astronomers to extract more information from the light their instruments collect.
"I feel we just unlocked a new frontier," Wang says. "We've now gone beyond the telescope stability limit for the first time with this new technique, and this new paradigm, I think, can be applied to every instrument that's trying to image exoplanets."
Bringing the Search for Alien Life Into Focus
For Bouman, the long-term ambition is much larger than simply finding more distant planets. Astronomers ultimately hope to obtain direct images of worlds resembling Earth and examine them for possible signs of life.
Reaching that goal will require major advances in telescope engineering, astronomical instruments, and image processing. But the new research demonstrates that some of the most important improvements may come from better ways of interpreting data rather than building increasingly precise hardware.
"There's still a long way to go, but this work shows how much more is possible when we combine advances in telescope technology with computational imaging," Bouman says. "Sometimes, the key to seeing something new isn't just building a better instrument but finding a better way to make sense of the light it collects."
The findings were published in Nature in a paper titled "Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit." Additional co-authors include William T. Freeman and Brandon Y. Feng of MIT, along with Laurent Pueyo and Marshall D. Perrin of the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore.
The research received support from the Space Telescope Science Institute, the Sloan Foundation, an Amazon AI4Science Discovery Award, and the National Science Foundation.
Story Source:
Materials provided by California Institute of Technology. Original written by Katie Neith. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, Jason J. Wang, Katherine L. Bouman, William T. Freeman, Laurent Pueyo, Brandon Y. Feng, Marshall D. Perrin. Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit. Nature, 2026; 659 (8139): 58 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z

articles.title: Double-catch drama: Why Starship's Flight 15 is so important to SpaceX
articles.text:
Double-catch drama: Why Starship's Flight 15 is so important to SpaceX
"This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary."
Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap.
Having reached orbit for the first time with Starship last time out, SpaceX is looking to take a huge stride toward full reusability with Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the megarocket's Ship upper stage, as the company eyes hourly launches by 2030.
SpaceX is targeting today (Nov. 13) for Starship's 15th flight, which will lift off from the company's Starbas site in South Texas. If all goes well, the mission — which you can watch here at Space.com — will end on Saturday (Nov. 14) with the first attempt at what SpaceX itself calls the "Holy Grail of rocketry": Catching both Starship's Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage chopstick-style back at the launch pad.
"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description.
The 75-minute Flight 15 launch window opens today at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), and a number of Starship firsts are planned for early in the flight. For example, while SpaceX has caught three Super Heavy boosters and reused two of them to date, the first attempt to catch a next-gen Super Heavy "V3" vehicle will come today, around 6.5 minutes after liftoff.
If the Ship upper stage gets the go-ahead for orbital insertion, it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites — designed especially for use on Starship — into low Earth orbit (LEO), starting about 35 minutes after launch. Then, 21 hours later, if "internally developed, and FAA-approved, conditions" for a return to Starbase and catch are met — including on-orbit assessment of Ship's heat shield by three of the V3 satellites — SpaceX will attempt to recover the orbital upper stage.
This landmark try will follow the first-ever Ship reentry over inhabited areas, as the vehicle will maneuver its way over sparsely populated regions of northern Mexico and southern Texas. (On previous missions, Ship has splashed down in the open ocean.) It will head back to Starbase and make a bellyflop maneuver as it descends to the site's Pad 2 before flipping itself vertical, ready for embrace of the launch tower's waiting mechanical arms.
"SpaceX will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship on the upcoming flight. If both are successful, it will mark the first time that all parts of an orbital rocket return to Earth intact," Elon Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Nov. 6. "This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary."
The catch
Half of the system is already proven. With catching and reflying boosters largely established, the next and unprecedented step is catching Ship. This is no easy task. The vehicle, returning from orbital speeds, must survive the heat of reentry, make its way precisely back to the pad put itself in position to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. The full recovery of an orbital launch system would, in the words of SpaceX, be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" and would open the "door to airplane-like cadence."
A successful catch would allow SpaceX to then work on refurbishing Ship for reflight, the next challenge of full reusability. Musk said in August in a SpaceX earnings call that the company will aim to refly the Super Heavy and Ship early next year.
SpaceX has a lot of experience with rocket reuse, as its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket pioneered the practice. But the company is eyeing another level of reflight with Starship: It's targeting roughly 10,000 launches of the megarocket per year by 2030, which works out to more than one launch per hour.
"We're aiming to reach 30+ Starship launches/day in 2030, which is ~10k annualized," Musk posted on X in August.
Why so many launches?
The company has repeated that figure to regulators. In comments filed with the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration in late October, it said that "SpaceX anticipates conducting 10,000 launches per year itself." Meanwhile, the recently signed National Space Transportation Policy aims to boost the U.S.'s capabilities to support more than 1,000 rocket launches per year by 2030.
Musk added that SpaceX's planned Starbase Louisiana site alone could support that many Starship launches. For context: SpaceX launched 165 Falcon 9 missions in 2025, and that was about half of the global total for orbital flights.
Why is SpaceX targeting this incredible increase in launch cadence? It wants to build satellite megaconstellations that dwarf anything the world has ever seen.
The company's V3 Starlink satellites are too large to fly efficiently on the Falcon 9. Each one of the next-gen spacecraft adds 1 terabit of capacity to SpaceX's broadband network, and the 26 flying on Flight 15 are equivalent to around 10 Falcon 9 launches packed with Starlink V2 Mini satellites, according to SpaceX. And the company wants to put a staggering 100,000 V3 Starlink satellites into orbit. (There are currently about 11,000 current-gen Starlink satellites in orbit, and that's by far the largest satellite network assembled to date.)
SpaceX's Starmind project blows even this figure out of the water. SpaceX wants to launch up to 1 million satellites to serve as orbital AI data centers, and it appears to be making the moves terrestrially regarding the hardware. On Nov. 10, German firm Singulus Technologies announced a contract worth more than 60 million euros for a solar cell production line for Starmind satellites, which SpaceX builds in Bastrop, Texas. Musk said the order covers equipment for 100 gigawatts of solar cells per year. In terms of orbital hardware, the project is only feasible if SpaceX can reach its targeted "airplane-like cadence."
The gap
The gap between SpaceX's vision and the situation today is vast. Starship flew four times in 2024 and five times in 2025, and Flight 15 would be its fourth launch of 2026. Musk said on the earnings call that he expects Starship to fly weekly at some point in the first half of 2027, and twice weekly or more by the end of that year. Starbase in Texas is currently authorized for 25 launches per year, and the Louisiana site is not expected to host a launch before 2029.
Even a perfect outing for Flight 15 and two clean catches will leave lots of work to do. SpaceX will then need to demonstrate reflight with Ship, after assessing the impact on its heat shield system. Then comes orbital refueling, which is a necessary step for any Starship trip beyond LEO and a requirement for SpaceX's commitment to NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. It's unclear how many tanker flights and refuelings will be needed to make a lunar mission possible, but, whatever the number, Starship will probably need to be rapidly reusable. Another step is carrying people. SpaceX has tested life support hardware on the ground in a crew cabin for the moon lander version of Starship that it is building for NASA, but no Starship has flown with such a system.
There are no guarantees for Flight 15. Ship will only be cleared for a return to Starbase and a catch attempt if it meets safety checks after reaching orbit, which itself is an achievement not to be taken for granted. Flight controllers may end up needing to bring Ship down in the Pacific Ocean or divert its reentry into the Gulf late into flight.
Musk told investors last month that success on this flight is "more likely than not." Whatever happens today and on Saturday, the measure of Starship's progress will soon shift from whether SpaceX can catch a Ship to how quickly it can launch one again.
Andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. He began writing for Space.com in 2019 and writes for SpaceNews, IEEE Spectrum, National Geographic, Sky & Telescope, New Scientist and others. Andrew first caught the space bug when, as a youngster, he saw Voyager images of other worlds in our solar system for the first time. Away from space, Andrew enjoys trail running in the forests of Finland. You can follow him on Twitter @AJ_FI.

articles.title: Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds
articles.text:
Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds
- Date:
- November 10, 2026
- Source:
- Cell Press
- Summary:
- A major review of more than 350 studies suggests that eating less protein could slow aging, improve metabolic health, and potentially extend lifespan, challenging the widespread belief that more protein is always better. Researchers warn that many sedentary adults may be consuming too much protein, while emphasizing that individual needs depend on age and physical activity.
- Share:
Protein is everywhere these days. From breakfast cereals and coffee to bottled water, manufacturers are adding extra protein to an expanding range of everyday products. But while consumers are being encouraged to eat more of it, a major scientific review suggests that cutting back on protein could offer surprising benefits for health and longevity.
After examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan. The potential benefits appear to involve several processes that influence how the body uses energy, responds to nutrients, protects cells from damage, and maintains healthy cellular function.
The findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets. Could many people be consuming far more protein than their bodies actually need?
"It's absolutely crystal clear that there are benefits of protein to muscle growth and exercise response of active individuals," says Dudley Lamming, the paper's corresponding author, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "But because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences."
Why Eating Less Protein Could Promote Longevity
Scientists have long understood that reducing calorie intake can extend lifespan in numerous organisms. Research has also linked calorie restriction to a lower risk of diseases associated with aging, including cancer. However, consistently eating fewer calories is challenging, making it difficult for many people to maintain such a diet over time.
An alternative approach has attracted increasing scientific interest: reducing protein without necessarily eating less food.
Experiments involving flies and rodents have demonstrated that limiting protein intake can increase lifespan even when total calorie consumption remains unchanged. This suggests that the benefits of dietary restriction may depend not only on how much food is consumed, but also on which nutrients make up that food.
Human research has produced encouraging findings as well. Several recent clinical trials have shown that people who reduce their protein intake can lose weight, decrease body fat, and improve fasting blood sugar levels, even when they consume more calories overall. Fasting blood sugar measures glucose in the bloodstream after a period without eating and is an important indicator of metabolic health.
These findings do not establish that protein restriction extends human lifespan, but they suggest that changing protein intake can influence processes associated with aging and disease.
The Debate Over How Much Protein We Really Need
The picture becomes more complicated when exercise and muscle health enter the equation.
Other studies have demonstrated that higher protein intake can support weight loss and help older adults preserve muscle mass, particularly when combined with physical activity. Maintaining muscle becomes increasingly important with age because muscle loss can contribute to weakness, reduced mobility, and a greater risk of falls.
Research highlighting these benefits helped motivate US authorities to revise dietary recommendations this year, encouraging daily protein consumption of 1.2-1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight (0.5-0.7 grams per pound). That represents nearly twice the previous recommended amount.
With protein consumption reaching new highs in the United States and older adults increasingly being advised to eat more, Lamming and a colleague examined decades of research to better understand the relationship between protein intake and aging.
Their analysis brought together findings from more than 350 papers, identifying several biological mechanisms that repeatedly appeared across studies. Together, these mechanisms suggest that lowering protein consumption may improve metabolic function, alter the way cells detect nutrients, limit cellular damage, and help preserve the processes that keep cells functioning properly.
A Hormone That May Help Explain Slower Aging
One particularly intriguing finding involves fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a hormone that becomes more abundant when dietary protein is limited.
FGF21 helps the body adjust to changes in nutrient availability and influences how energy is used. Higher levels of this hormone can increase energy expenditure, support healthier blood sugar regulation, and reduce inflammation.
These effects are especially interesting because metabolism and chronic inflammation are closely connected to aging. Over time, disruptions in these processes can contribute to conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and other age-related diseases.
Studies in mice have shown that animals with elevated FGF21 levels live longer than mice with normal levels. The lifespan benefit was particularly strong in males, suggesting that biological sex may influence how the body responds to this hormone.
Researchers have also established that eating less protein increases FGF21 levels in humans. Whether this hormonal response produces the same longevity benefits seen in mice remains an important unanswered question.
How Certain Amino Acids Could Influence Aging
The amount of protein someone eats may not be the only factor that matters. The types of amino acids that make up that protein could also play an important role.
Amino acids are the building blocks the body uses to produce proteins, which are essential for maintaining muscles, repairing tissues, and carrying out countless cellular functions. Beyond these basic roles, certain amino acids also act as signals that influence metabolism and cellular growth.
The review identifies three amino acids that appear especially important: methionine, isoleucine, and valine.
Research suggests that excessive intake of these amino acids can stimulate biological pathways that encourage growth. Although growth-related processes are essential for normal development and tissue repair, excessive or prolonged activation of certain pathways may contribute to obesity, inflammation, and other conditions associated with aging.
Limiting specific amino acids could therefore produce some of the benefits observed in protein-restricted diets. This possibility has attracted attention because it suggests that the relationship between protein and longevity may be more complicated than simply eating more or less of a single nutrient.
"These studies show that the amount of protein sedentary people are eating today may have negative health consequences, at least at the population level," Lamming says.
Why Exercise Could Change the Effects of Protein
The researchers emphasize that protein requirements are not the same for everyone.
Pregnant women, for example, need additional protein to support fetal development, while some older adults require higher amounts to help maintain muscle and physical function. People who exercise regularly may also benefit from greater protein consumption because their muscles use those nutrients to recover, repair tissue, and adapt to training.
For many adults who spend most of their day sitting, however, adding protein to everyday foods may offer little additional benefit.
Lamming points out that athletes frequently consume large amounts of protein without developing the metabolic diseases sometimes associated with protein-rich diets. One possible explanation is that physical activity changes how the body handles those nutrients.
Regular exercise stimulates muscle growth and repair, potentially allowing the body to put additional protein to productive use while reducing some of the harmful metabolic effects associated with high protein intake.
This distinction may help explain why studies sometimes reach seemingly contradictory conclusions about protein. A diet that benefits someone who exercises intensely may not be ideal for someone with a largely sedentary lifestyle.
Rather than recommending the same amount of protein for everyone, the researchers argue that dietary advice should better reflect individual circumstances, especially physical activity levels and age.
"Recent recommendations have encouraged people to eat more protein, but they've also encouraged people to exercise more," Lamming says. "We probably need to personalize protein recommendations based not just on age, but also on how physically active people are."
The findings challenge the assumption that adding more protein automatically leads to better health. Although protein remains essential, the growing body of longevity research suggests that for some people, consuming less may offer benefits that have been overlooked in the rush toward protein-rich foods.
The work was supported by the National Institute on Aging, the Wisconsin Partnership Program, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cell Press. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Bailey A. Knopf, Dudley W. Lamming. The hallmarks of protein and amino acid restriction in aging and longevity. Cell Press Blue, 2026; 1 (5): 100079 DOI: 10.1016/j.cpblue.2026.100079

articles.title: Scientists discover two adorable species of howler monkey in the Amazon — they're already endangered
articles.text:
Scientists discover two adorable species of howler monkey in the Amazon — and they're already endangered
A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.
Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.
The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.
"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.
One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.
In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.
Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.
For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.
The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.

articles.title: Powerful Vulcan Centaur rocket launching for 1st time in 9 months Nov. 14: Watch it live
articles.text:
Powerful Vulcan Centaur rocket launching for 1st time in 9 months Nov. 14: Watch it live
Update: United Launch Alliance has delayed the launch of its Vulcan Centaur rocket to Saturday (Nov. 14) at 12:32 p.m. ET (1732 GMT) due to a power issue in a liquid gaseous nitrogen factory that pumps propellant into the rocket. "The vehicle and spacecraft are healthy," ULA wrote in an update on X.
United Launch Alliance's (ULA) Vulcan Centaur rocket will fly on Saturday (Nov. 14) for the first time in nine months, and you can watch the action live.
A Vulcan Centaur topped with 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites is scheduled to lift off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Nov. 14 at 12:32 p.m. ET (1732 GMT).
You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of ULA, or directly via the company. Coverage will start 20 minutes before liftoff.
Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which has just a half-dozen launches left on its manifest.
Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and has flown three more times since. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024, and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs).
In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addresses the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.)
ULA has been working hard on that front, and the company is confident that Vulcan is ready to return to flight.
"The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update.
"To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission," ULA added. "By flying the improved design, ULA gains valuable flight data that validates these improvements and is the most beneficial path in support of all our customers."
Saturday's launch will help build out Amazon's broadband constellation in low Earth orbit (LEO), which was previously called Project Kuiper but is now known as Amazon Leo. It will eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink network, which has been up and running for several years.
Amazon Leo will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. About 400 of them have reached space to date on 15 launches, which have been conducted by three different rockets — the Atlas V, SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. Today's launch will be the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1.
If all goes according to plan Saturday, Vulcan Centaur will deploy the 40 Amazon Leo satellites over a 25-minute span beginning about 70 minutes after launch. They'll be released roughly 270 miles (435 kilometers) above our planet.
The Amazon Leo launch could be part of a very busy 12-hour stretch. SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on Friday (Nov. 13), on a test mission that will feature the first-ever catch attempt of the vehicle's Ship upper stage. And Rocket Lab is scheduled to launch its 100th-ever mission at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT) on Saturday (Nov. 14).
You can watch all of this action live here at Space.com when the time comes.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title: ‘Godless’ philosopher Jeremy Bentham, who died nearly 200 years ago, had severe dental problems
articles.text:
'Godless' founder of utilitarianism had severe dental problems and was in 'excruciating pain,' CT scans of his severed head reveal
Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.
The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.
The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.
The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.
Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.
As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.
Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.
Brainless auto-icon
To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.
Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.
The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."
"Godless" philosopher
Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.
Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."
His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.
Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."
This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.
Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

articles.title: Global fossil fuel emissions set to fall in 2026, but total CO2 keeps rising
articles.text:
Global fossil fuel emissions set to fall in 2026, but total CO2 keeps rising
- Date:
- November 10, 2026
- Source:
- University of Exeter
- Summary:
- Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall in 2026 as renewable energy and electric vehicles gain ground, but rising emissions from deforestation threaten to push total CO2 emissions to a new record. Scientists warn that the world's remaining carbon budget for limiting warming to 1.5°C could be exhausted in less than four years, even as a lasting decline in emissions appears increasingly within reach.
- Share:
Global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels are expected to decline slightly in 2026, offering a promising sign that the world's transition to cleaner energy is beginning to make a measurable difference. According to the latest Global Carbon Budget from the Global Carbon Project, fossil fuel CO2 emissions are projected to fall by 0.4%, partly because of growing solar and wind power generation and disruptions linked to the Iran conflict.
The report estimates that fossil fuel emissions will total 38.2 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) in 2026. Oil emissions alone are expected to drop by 1.9%, largely reflecting a temporary energy shock associated with the conflict.
Clean energy is also playing an increasingly important role. Although worldwide energy consumption continues to grow, solar power, wind power, and electric vehicles are now meeting roughly two-thirds of the additional demand. Even so, researchers caution that the transition is not happening quickly enough to guarantee a lasting reduction in fossil fuel emissions.
Fossil Fuel Emissions Fall, but Total CO2 Keeps Rising
Despite the projected decline in fossil fuel emissions, the overall picture is more troubling. When emissions from land-use change (such as deforestation) are included, total global CO2 emissions are expected to reach 43.3 billion metric tons in 2026, compared with 42.8 billion metric tons in 2025.
That increase highlights how progress in cleaner energy can be undermined by continued forest loss and other changes to the landscape.
The report also delivers a stark warning about the world's remaining carbon budget (the amount of CO2 that can be emitted before warming reaches 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels). Researchers estimate that just 150 billion metric tons remain, enough for less than four years at today's emission rates.
As carbon dioxide continues accumulating in the atmosphere, the risks and damaging consequences of climate change are becoming more severe.
Natural Carbon Sinks Face New Climate Pressures
Beyond tracking emissions, the researchers examined the planet's natural "sinks" (absorption of CO2 by land and ocean). These natural systems help limit atmospheric carbon dioxide by taking up some of what human activities release.
The amount of carbon absorbed by land ecosystems has recovered to earlier levels after weakening substantially during the 2023-24 El Niño weather pattern. However, scientists expect the powerful 2026 El Niño to significantly influence carbon absorption in the coming year.
The research brought together experts from the University of Exeter, the University of East Anglia (UEA), the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, Ludwig-Maximilian-University Munich (LMU), the Alfred-Wegener-Institut, and more than 90 additional institutions worldwide.
Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, who directs the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter and led the research, emphasized that a temporary reduction in emissions is not enough.
"A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution."
"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline."
Clean Energy Could Bring a Historic Turning Point
Despite the challenges, researchers see growing evidence that renewable energy and electric transportation are beginning to change the trajectory of global emissions.
Professor Corinne Le Quéré, Royal Society Research Professor at UEA's School of Environmental Sciences, pointed to the expanding influence of clean technologies, particularly in China.
"Clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions. Solar and wind power and electric vehicles are expanding rapidly, led by China. Countries on every continent are decreasing their emissions while growing their economies. A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years."
However, a single year of falling emissions does not necessarily mean the world has reached a lasting peak. Glen Peters, Research Professor at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, stressed the importance of changes that permanently reduce reliance on fossil fuels.
"A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries, and electric vehicles is pushing emissions down in dozens of countries and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions."
Researchers also emphasize that reducing emissions alone will not be sufficient. Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere must become a much larger part of climate strategies.
Professor Julia Pongratz of LMU's Department of Geography explained the challenge:
"Alongside reducing emissions, we need to scale up CO2 removal to reach greenhouse gas neutrality. Afforestation and reforestation already remove substantial amounts of CO2, but these gains are still more than offset by emissions from deforestation, and novel carbon removal remains very limited. We need to act on all these fronts now."
Carbon Emissions in China, the US, India, and Europe
The 2026 Global Carbon Budget reveals significant differences in how emissions are changing across major economies.
China, which accounts for approximately 32% of the world's fossil fuel emissions, is expected to record a 0.9% reduction in 2026 after two consecutive years of relatively slow emissions growth. A substantial decline in oil emissions is helping drive the decrease, although emissions from coal are projected to rise slightly by 0.3%.
At the same time, China continues rapidly expanding electricity generation from renewable sources. The country leads the world in deploying clean technologies and expanding carbon absorption through reforestation. About half of the emissions avoided globally through renewable energy and electric vehicles can be attributed to China. It also has the largest carbon uptake from reforestation and afforestation (new forests).
The United States is projected to reduce emissions by 1.3%, primarily because of lower coal use. Coal emissions increased in 2025 as elevated natural gas prices and cold weather encouraged greater reliance on coal.
India is moving in the opposite direction. Its fossil fuel emissions are expected to grow by 4.4% in 2026, exceeding its average annual growth rate of 3.5% over the past decade.
Elsewhere, the European Union is projected to cut emissions by 1.5%, while Japan is expected to record a 1% reduction.
Taken together, countries outside these major economies are forecast to reduce emissions by 0.7%. Much of that decrease comes from lower oil consumption, likely reflecting higher prices and restrictions on global supplies.
Oil Emissions Decline as Coal Continues to Rise
The report also provides a breakdown of projected emissions from individual fossil fuels.
Oil is expected to experience the largest reduction, with emissions falling 1.9% in 2026. Natural gas emissions are projected to decrease by 0.3%, while coal emissions are expected to increase by 0.6%.
International transportation is also contributing to the overall decline. Emissions from international aviation and international shipping are each forecast to fall by 1%. Reduced aviation activity in the Middle East is partly responsible for the decrease in air travel emissions.
Although these developments help slow fossil fuel emissions, the report indicates that much of the progress remains vulnerable to economic and geopolitical changes.
Deforestation Threatens Global Climate Progress
One of the report's most concerning findings involves carbon emissions from changes in land use.
Although emissions from land-use change have generally declined over the past decade, they are expected to increase to 5.1 billion metric tons of CO2 in 2026.
The projected rise is linked to increased peat fires (almost entirely ignited by human activities) and the degradation of forests in Southeast Asia. Drier conditions associated with the developing El Niño have contributed to these problems.
Even with the latest increase, the long-term growth of total emissions has slowed considerably. Over the past decade, combined emissions from fossil fuels and land-use change increased by an average of 0.3% annually (0.3% per year), compared with 1.7% annually during the preceding decade (1.7% per year).
Permanent deforestation remains a major source of carbon dioxide. Between 2016 and 2025, it released approximately 3.8 billion metric tons of CO2 each year. Reforestation and the establishment of new forests remove substantial amounts of carbon, but these activities offset only about half the emissions associated with permanent deforestation.
China, the 27 countries of the European Union, and the United States together account for the largest carbon removals through reforestation and afforestation, absorbing approximately 0.8 billion metric tons of CO2 annually.
Brazil, Russia, and Indonesia also absorb considerable carbon through forest growth and restoration. However, in those countries, emissions from deforestation outweigh the benefits.
Emerging technologies designed to remove carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere or through other new approaches are making only a tiny contribution. At their current scale, these methods (excluding conventional means such as reforestation) compensate for less than 30 minutes of annual fossil fuel CO2 emissions.
Meanwhile, the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide is projected to reach 427.7 parts per million in 2026, approximately 54% higher than before the Industrial Revolution.
More Countries Are Growing Their Economies While Cutting Emissions
A separate analysis by the same researchers, currently in press in another peer-reviewed journal, offers additional evidence that the expansion of clean energy is changing the relationship between economic growth and carbon emissions.
As global energy demand increases, solar power, wind power, and electric vehicles can prevent some of that additional consumption from producing new fossil fuel emissions (or "offset").
Looking ahead through the end of 2028, the researchers estimate that expanding clean technologies will offset between 64% and 79% of the emissions that would otherwise result from growing energy demand.
Another encouraging trend is the increasing number of countries reducing emissions while their economies continue to expand.
According to the analysis, 59 countries had lower emissions in 2025 than in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic, even as their economies grew.
The benefits are not limited to countries where emissions have already begun declining. Between 2019 and 2025, every major world region experienced slower emissions growth, including China, India, and other emerging economies where total emissions continued to rise.
Solar, Wind, and Electric Vehicles Are Reshaping Emissions
Electric vehicles are making an increasingly important contribution to reducing emissions, although their overall impact is still limited by the time required to replace existing gasoline and diesel vehicles.
In 2025, approximately 10% of the global car fleet was electrified (or 6% excluding hybrids). As more conventional vehicles are replaced, electric transportation is expected to play a larger role in reducing fossil fuel consumption.
Solar and wind power are already producing much more substantial benefits.
In 2010, these renewable energy sources prevented an estimated 0.28 billion metric tons of CO2 emissions. By 2025, that figure had climbed to 4.1 billion metric tons, and it is projected to reach 4.6 billion metric tons in 2026.
The sharp increase demonstrates how quickly cleaner electricity generation is expanding and how much additional pollution would be produced without it.
The researchers believe that continued progress could bring the world to a critical milestone sooner than many might expect.
"If further acceleration of clean technology deployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away."
The Global Carbon Budget is compiled annually by an international collaboration of more than 140 scientists. It provides a transparent assessment of global carbon emissions using established scientific methods and undergoes peer review.
The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is scheduled for publication as a preprint in Earth System Science Data on November 10, with a peer-reviewed version to follow.

articles.title: 'Don't panic': SpaceX pens familiar message on Starship ahead of historic double-catch test flight
articles.text:
'Don't panic': SpaceX pens familiar message on Starship ahead of historic double-catch test flight
SpaceX has a message for itself, and for the spacecraft set to make history today (Nov. 13): Don't panic.
The company's Starship megarocket will conduct its 15th test flight this afternoon, a landmark liftoff that will feature the first-ever attempt to catch both of its stages with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms.
On Thursday (Nov. 12), SpaceX rolled the Flight 15 upper stage, a vehicle known as Ship 42, out to the launch pad at its Starbase site in South Texas to prep. The company shared photos of the move on X, and in two of those shots we can see some intriguing words inked on the spacecraft: "Don't panic."
The phrase is familiar to fans of Douglas Adams' sci-fi classic "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy": In the novel, the electronic guidebook that helps travelers find their way across the cosmos has "Don't panic!" on its cover.
And Ship 42 itself is connected to the beloved book, by virtue of its serial number. In "The Hitchhiker's Guide," a supercomputer named Deep Mind is asked to come up with "the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything." It thinks for 7.5 million years and comes up with "42."
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk has voiced his affection for "The Hitchhiker's Guide" in the past — and he has already paid tribute to it with a well-placed "Don't panic."
The debut launch of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket back in February 2018 sent Musk's red Tesla Roadster into orbit around the sun, with a spacesuit-clad mannequin named Starman at the wheel and its entertainment display programmed to read "Don't panic!"
Starship Flight 15 is scheduled to launch today during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). You can watch it here at Space.com.
If all goes according to plan, Starship's Super Heavy first stage will come back to Starbase for a chopsticks catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.
Ship 42, meanwhile, will head to orbit, a destination that Starship reached for the first time on Flight 14, which took place on Sept. 28. Ship 42 will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites today — the second batch of the spacecraft to reach orbit. (The first set of 26 were delivered on Flight 14).
Ship 42 will stay up for a while after that, circling Earth 14 times before coming back for its own chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after launch.
That's the plan, anyway; SpaceX will only go through with a Ship catch attempt if all systems on the vehicle look good. If there are any problems, the company will divert to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, near either Hawaii or Chile.
Both of Starship's stages — Super Heavy and the Ship — are designed to be rapidly reusable. And "rapidly" is a bit of understatement: SpaceX wants to launch 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030, Musk has said.
The chopsticks-catch strategy is a big part of that vision. Bringing both Starship stages directly back to the launch mount will greatly reduce the time needed for inspection, refurbishment and reflight, according to SpaceX.
The company has already caught Super Heavy on three previous Starship test flights. It has never tried to do so with Ship, instead targeting ocean splashdowns with the upper stage.
The double catch attempt may be unprecedented, but SpaceX seems to be taking its own advice: There's no panic around Flight 15 or its bold goals.
"I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," Musk said last month, during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title: 1,800-year-old bronze foot found in bog was carefully taken from a giant Roman emperor statue in Scotland
articles.text:
Romans carefully dismantled statue of emperor when they withdrew from Scotland 1,800 years ago, leaving only his foot behind
A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.
All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.
The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.
Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.
This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.
Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.
During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."
"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.
"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."
But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?
The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.
From Augustus to Nero, see how much you know about ancient Rome's famous leaders with our Roman emperor quiz!
Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.
