articles.title: Trump doesn’t plan to raise Nvidia, spy issue during China trip: U.S. officials
articles.text:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed, a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

articles.title: SpaceX launches Starship in key test flight of massive rocket
articles.text:
In a key test flight on Friday, SpaceX tried but failed to recover both stages of its massive Starship rocket.
The rocket lifted off from the company's South Texas launch facility at 4:47 p.m. local time, or 5:47 p.m. ET. SpaceX had to abort its plans to catch and reuse the booster, instead diverting it to splash into the Gulf of Mexico, where it burst into flames.
Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship mission to date, was the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the booster and upper stage, or spacecraft portion, of the massive rocket.
Earlier on Friday, SpaceX obtained authorization from the Federal Aviation Administration. Hours later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after reporting communication problems affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers. The SpaceX license wasn't effected by the flight stoppage, a spokesperson for the FAA told CNBC.
The upper stage of the Starship continued its trajectory into orbit after the company failed to catch and salvage the booster. The rocket is expected to fly around the Earth fourteen times in total. If successful, SpaceX will land the upper stage back at its Starbase facility on Saturday.
Starship's success is critical to SpaceX and its ambitions to eventually lift cargo and people to the surface of the Moon and Mars. In the near-term, SpaceX needs to send more satellites into orbit to expands its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center.
The company's constellation already includes over 11,000 active satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket has the capacity to carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, the company has said, representing about 20 times the capacity of earlier Falcon 9 rockets.
In the previous Starship test flight, the company released 26 v3 satellites, and released another 26 in the Friday test flight, with the goal of "Starlink becoming 51% of the internet," SpaceX said in a post on X.
When it comes to launches, "SpaceX is likely a full decade ahead of peers on this front," William Blair analysts wrote in a note out on Friday. "Even if tonight's catch is unsuccessful, a delay by a few months is not that consequential."
Meanwhile, SpaceX is facing fresh criticism over restrictions imposed on its Starshield satellite internet service in Ukraine. Starshield is built on Starlink technology and is the military-tier of SpaceX's satellite internet service.
Earlier this week, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country's military forces had experienced limits on Starshield without warning again, harming their ability to defend against Russia's ongoing aerial attacks. Similar limits on Starshield in Ukraine were temporarily imposed last month.
Some U.S. senators have condemned the restrictions, and urged Congress to investigate SpaceX.

articles.title: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance—2 habits that take 'a few seconds' can help you avoid similar traps
articles.text:
The biggest heist in cryptocurrency history began with small mistakes many internet users make. A hacking group tied to North Korea recently stole $6.3 billion from the crypto exchange Binance. The operation was sophisticated, involving fake job interviews and malicious code.
But it was also mundane. Although artificial intelligence played a role in the hack, this was not a cyberattack of the future, propelled by swarms of AI agents. Rather, it relied on humans who made some basic errors, like clicking a link because it appeared first on a search results page or trusting strangers at a fake company without taking a few seconds to look them up.
We work at the Digital Inquiry Group, a nonprofit that researches how people evaluate online information and creates free, evidence-based curriculum that helps people decide what to trust.
In over a decade of research, we've found that people frequently engage in online behavior that makes them more likely to get duped. Two simple strategies can help you better navigate today's information landscape, from traditional phishing to misleading social posts to AI fakes. Here's how.
When searching online, the first result is not always the best or the safest
The Binance heist began when one of the company's engineers downloaded compromised software. That engineer, according to the Reuters investigation of the hack, clicked on a sponsored search result that appeared higher on the results page and directed them to the malicious code.
Our research at the Digital Inquiry Group suggests internet users frequently behave as if first is best. They click on the first thing they see. They incorrectly associate a higher placement with vetted content, ceding judgment to tech company algorithms. Students have gone so far as to tell us "Google is almost never wrong" or "AI is always right."
Professional fact-checkers commonly practice click restraint. They understand that whether you're searching on the internet or querying a chatbot, first isn't always best. If you're researching an organization, the first link will often be to its own site, which is hardly likely to disclose anything that's wrong with it.
So the next time you search for something online, be wary of links to sponsored content, the organization you're investigating, or to open platforms where anyone can post and information isn't verified, such as Quora or Reddit. Read the brief snippets beneath each link, and make a more informed choice about what to open.
Always ask yourself: Who is behind this information? What makes them credible? Look for people and organizations that have direct expertise on the topic at hand, or have processes to ensure the accuracy of information, such as news outlets that employ editors and fact-checkers.
'The internet is a precarious place'—always get external verification
Binance says it caught that first malicious download, replaced the device and changed passwords. But later, another engineer downloaded compromised code as part of what they thought was a job interview, which included a virtual meeting with the supposed CEO of a fake company.
It's tempting to think that the engineer should have seen something was off. But the internet is a precarious place because bad actors know how to make content feel legitimate. Binance says its employee was snared by a hacker posing as an HR rep who "shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust."
When they encounter a piece of unfamiliar content, professional fact-checkers don't just read it closely — they read laterally. They open new browser tabs to see what other, credible sources have to say. Fact-checkers know that bad actors make themselves look good on their home turf, but that it's a lot harder to fake a good reputation across the internet.
The next time you encounter something unfamiliar online, look for authoritative sources that can shed light on the person or organization. You might find a news article that confirms the claim you're looking into, or a report that identifies a supposedly neutral source as biased.
In some cases, you may find nothing at all, which is a signal in itself: if you look up a company that reached out to you and find no external confirmation of its existence, that should be an immediate red flag.
Had that first Binance engineer engaged in click restraint and verified the source of the software, they might have avoided the malicious download. Had that second employee taken time to seek external verification about the supposed HR rep, rather than trusting a polished social media profile, they might have realized that something didn't add up.
The internet and AI have made it harder to know whether what we see is authentic. They've also made it easier than ever before to investigate who or what we encounter online. It's always worth pausing to check. A few seconds up front can save us all a lot of time, grief and money later on.
Nadav Ziv is a researcher at the Digital Inquiry Group. Joel Breakstone is co-founder and executive director of the Digital Inquiry Group.

articles.title: Nvidia is done with Jensen Huang. The fallout in Washington is just beginning
articles.text:
Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded.
Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.
Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat.
"In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday.
Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump's crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China.
Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal.
The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department.
By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick to testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement.
Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers."
And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress.
The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls
Warren and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks.
Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. It would likely include his committee, as well as the House intelligence panel and the House Permanent Select Committee on China, and it would be under oath and transcribed. It's not clear at this point whether it would be public.
"We want to see him basically in a week … Sooner rather than later," Mast told reporters Thursday, adding that he believed it would happen before Thanksgiving.
If Huang doesn't willingly appear, Mast said he will subpoena him.
Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., sent a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast also sent a second request to Kessler.
Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair.
"From an intelligence committee perspective, you can imagine from an AI perspective, how important this is for our national security, for our critical infrastructure and understand when it comes to chip policy, what exactly got to China and ... did Megaspeed divert chips?" Gottheimer said.
The calls for immediate investigation into Huang and Nvidia on the day of his resignation represent a stunning fall from grace in the halls of power for the former CEO. Huang was one of the most effective voices for the AI industry in Washington — able to toggle between leveraging his relationship with Trump and defending his industry from fears about AI's risks to lawmakers.
"He is always the TED Talk guy," one senior Democratic staff member who was granted anonymity to describe private meetings they had attended with Huang, told CNBC. "He's really good and articulate, and really good at explaining why AI is important and why it's so important for the United States to be leading here."
The staffer said Huang was a "happy warrior" for AI, and stayed longer than scheduled or anticipated for questions from lawmakers. But in the meetings with lawmakers the aide attended, they said Huang did not aggressively push against export controls or get too "deep in the weeds" to really "lobby one way or the other" with the lawmakers.
Huang has repeatedly resisted export controls publicly, a move that has rubbed some lawmakers the wrong way.
Some lawmakers even lamented the loss of Huang, despite the inevitable buzzsaw he now faces on Capitol Hill.
"It's just sad all around," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said of Huang's resignation.

articles.title: The AI trade faces big tests next week, starting with Nvidia earnings and capped by Anthropic IPO
articles.text: The artificial intelligence trade is about to face its next big test in the week ahead, with Nvidia earnings and Anthropic 's IPO on the docket. Stocks held up surprisingly well this week, especially considering Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's exit — following affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two company employees — led some to worry that Wall Street's AI heavyweight was about to dive 20% or more . Instead, the chipmaker ended the week down by about 13%, while the major averages themselves scored their best week since August . The S & P 500 technology sector is higher by more than 2%, snapping a five-week slump. Far from abandoning the AI trade, investors instead rotated into other tech stocks, such as Apple , Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom that bulls took as a sign of health in the market — one where gains are dispersing elsewhere. "The Nvidia story is now idiosyncratic," said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide Investment Management Group. "There's a lot of nervousness priced in right now, and the good news is, the market has proven its ability to withstand idiosyncratic but painful moves in tech." With traders hopeful the stock market has set the stage for a short-term bounce, there are two catalysts next week that could either revive or snuff out the AI recovery. Tuning into Nvidia Nvidia's earnings Tuesday after the market closes will be watched closely. Results are widely expected to meet high expectations. Investors will listen closely for any clarity on the company's succession plans now that Huang has left and been replaced by chief financial officer and interim CEO Colette Kress. The 13-year veteran of Nvidia, who served earlier stints at Cisco and Microsoft, may lack the showmanship and panache of her predecessor, but can soothe investors looking for a steady hand to steer the ship until a successor is named. Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, is emerging as an early favorite. More importantly, traders are closely watching for opportunities to get in on Nvidia, after its more than 30% decline in six weeks, which obliterated roughly $2 trillion from its market value. Other investors are still wary there's more to come. Jeff Kilburg, founder of KKM Financial, said the opportunity now is to buy and own Nvidia. To define his risk, he said he bought January $200 calls this week. The stock was last at about $160. "There's a ton of uncertainty, and I'm not trying to pretend like I know anything," Kilburg said. "But what I do know is that the line of sight is that they have a trillion dollars in demand verified, and that trillion dollars in demand, which takes them through 2028 between Blackwell and Ruben, that's not going away." "I have confidence that the company is going to find a way through," Kilburg added. Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co, has a 12-month price target of $225 on Nvidia without Huang as CEO. Given where Nvidia is trading, he considers it a buying opportunity. AI temperature check Anthropic could also give investors a temperature check, if its debut next week is met enthusiastically by traders. The stock is expected to start trading Thursday on the Nasdaq Global Select Market after pricing its IPO Wednesday in an expected range of $70 to $78 per share. It's supposed to start trading under the ticker "ANT." If Anthropic debuts as expected next week, the AI laboratory will do so after lowering its estimated valuation to about $1.2 trillion from $2 trillion earlier in the fall, a wise move for the company, according to Benjamin Black, investment chief at Powerlaw Corp., a publicly traded, closed-end investment fund. The money manager said Anthropic is "not even really that expensive," given that the company is supposed to reach a $100 billion annualized revenue run rate by the end of 2026, meaning the price would pencil out at roughly 12 times ARR. "I have never seen a company that had more demand from investors to get into than than Anthropic in the private market," Black said. "Anthropic's smart to give up some price to make it easy for the public to make some money here," he continued. "I think at that price, it's going to do quite well." Week ahead calendar All times ET. articles.title: FAA lifts ground stop after four hours, but flight cancellations will stretch into the weekend
articles.text:
The Federal Aviation Administration halted flight departures across the country for more than four hours on Friday, the second time it had issued a nationwide ground stop since 9/11, blaming communications failures that affected multiple air traffic control centers. More than 10,000 flights were disrupted, with delays and cancellations set to stretch into the weekend.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed aging air traffic control infrastructure for the problem.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday at the White House that there was no indication that the issues were a threat to the United States. He later said at a press conference that it doesn't appear to be a cyber attack, and that it "appears this was mechanically driven."
The FAA canceled the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday.
The agency earlier said in post on X that there was a "temporary telecommunications outage" and that it halted flights out of an "abundance of caution."
While the FAA lifted the ground stop, travel chaos continued at airports, which were forced to find places for parked planes. Delays were set to continue.
Carriers were preparing to cancel flights as the disruption wore on. JetBlue Airways told staff it would cancel the remainder of the day's flights, aside from European routes, as well as others scheduled for Saturday so that crews and planes are in place to resume operations, according to a memo seen by CNBC.
A ground stop halts flights at their departure point. Disruptions tend to snowball if ground stops drag on as flight crews reach their maximum number of duty hours for a day.
There were 11,000 flights scheduled to depart U.S. airports after 4 p.m. ET on Friday, according to flight-data firm Cirium. There were about 600 diverted flights on Friday, 104 of them sent to other airports, Cirium said.
International flights had started taking off from coastal hubs before 6 p.m. ET.
Flights will be allowed to depart as en route traffic facilities recover, "through coordination with the air traffic control system," the FAA said earlier.
When it issued the ground stop at about 4 p.m., the FAA said the communications issues were "impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers." These facilities guide airplanes at high altitudes along their routes.
The FAA's technicians are investigating, the agency said.
Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare.
In January 2023, the FAA halted flights because of issues with a pilot alert system. Before that, traffic was halted nationwide after the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.
Aging technology
Technical issues have repeatedly snarled air traffic in the U.S. in recent years.
In September, hundreds of flights into Newark, New Jersey, and Philadelphia were canceled, delayed or diverted after a Verizon fiber cable was accidentally cut. Officials said it occurred during construction in New Jersey, severing a backup feed of key data for air traffic controllers.
In 2025, air traffic controllers lost contact with aircraft heading to and from Newark Liberty International Airport, an equipment failure that led to massive flight delays and raised more concerns about aging U.S. aviation infrastructure and staffing shortages.
"It's going to continue to fail," Duffy said of U.S. air traffic control infrastructure. The U.S. is in the middle of an overhaul of the technology, and Duffy urged lawmakers for more funding on Friday.
Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis, the FAA said.
The major U.S. airlines issued statements saying they would work with customers who were affected by the ground stop and encouraged travelers to check for updates.
— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger and Phil LeBeau contributed to this article.

articles.title: AI risks are the biggest threat to the financial system, Fed survey finds
articles.text:
Threats from artificial intelligence topped the list for greatest risks to the financial system, far exceeding any other dangers, according to respondents who participated in a Federal Reserve survey released Friday.
The central bank's twice-yearly look at a variety of dangers saw a surge in respondents saying that the biggest danger comes from AI along several fronts including debt, stock market valuations and security risks.
"Respondents noted three distinct areas of concern: (1) elevated equity valuations and the possibility that lower-than-expected earnings could result in lower valuations and a market correction; (2) cybersecurity risk, stemming from either a malicious attack by sophisticated state actors or damage caused by frontier AI models themselves; and (3) risks associated with complex forms of AI-related financing," the report stated.
The report comes with Wall Street on edge over high-flying AI hyperscalers, while communities are on alert for the rapid spread of data centers used to power the technology. Some 56% of voters in this month's midterm elections said data centers were of crucial or major importance in their choices, according to exit polling.
Respondents to the Fed survey released Friday include a variety of market participants, economists, analysts and institutional sources. The report covers the period up to Oct. 28, just a few days shy of the election.
Of the group, 87% cited AI as a "salient risk" to the system. That was up from 50% in the survey during the spring of this year and well ahead of the next most-cited danger, a risk asset correction, which was mentioned by 52% of those surveyed.
Other leading risks were higher long-term rates (48%), cyberattacks (43%) and fiscal debt sustainability (43%), the latter coming with the U.S. debt over $40 trillion and the budget deficit near $2 trillion.
The report otherwise found the system fairly stable, though it mentioned that hedge fund leverage is at its highest since 2013 and concentrated on a relatively small group.

articles.title: They train people to avoid 'honeypot' scams—here are the common red flags they spot: 'It feels so good to be wanted'
articles.text:
Shawnee Delaney often kicks off a training session by telling a room full of corporate workers: "OK, raise your hand if you've ever gotten a flattering message on LinkedIn just complimenting your background and your profile and your experience."
"Every hand goes up," she says. Then, she tells attendees how responding to a simple adulatory message could unwittingly open the door to a potential romance scam.
Delaney is a corporate security expert, well-versed in teaching people how to avoid “honeypot” schemes, in which a bad actor uses romantic or sexual interest to build trust and gain information, access or leverage over a target. The term is currently making headlines in the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation from the company, following reporting on his admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Honeypots, also known as "honey traps," are a very human form of social engineering attack, a category that also includes various forms of phishing and use of deepfake technology. And you don't have to be a billionaire tech CEO to possess information that scammers may value.
As competition in the global artificial intelligence race heats up, OpenAI is reportedly training employees to recognize espionage tactics including bribery, romantic manipulation and blackmail, according to The Wall Street Journal. On Nov. 3, cryptocurrency exchange Binance revealed that a recent cyberattack — which saw roughly $6 billion of digital assets stolen — was partially made possible by a fake job interview scheme that infected an employee’s work computer with malware.
"People can get solicited, bribed, romanced, etc.," says Kevin Tian, co-founder and CEO of Doppel, an AI-powered platform meant to help identify and deflect social engineering attacks. He adds: "If you've got access to sensitive IP [intellectual property] — it's not just AI companies — you can be a target."
Increasingly, scammers can use AI to scour websites ranging from Reddit to Pinterest for an individual's personal information and customize a ploy designed specifically for them, Tian says. Once they have relevant data points, attackers tend to use "the oldest tricks in the book: elicitation, flattery, ego," says Delaney, a former intelligence officer with the Defense Intelligence Agency and the founder and CEO of Washington, D.C.-based corporate security consulting firm Vaillance Group.
In many cases, Delaney notes, targets have an inkling that something is suspicious — but they'd rather allow themselves to believe the interest is legitimate. So how do you keep yourself from falling victim? Trust your self-awareness, common sense and ability to identify situations that feel too good to be true, she says.
"The bottom line is, we're all human," says Delaney, adding: "It feels so good to be wanted, or to be respected, or to be appreciated, or loved."
How to spot red flags and do some vetting
Delaney, who has worked with Fortune 500 companies such as Uber and Merck, advises corporate clients on cybersecurity risks and develops training programs to improve employees' awareness of security threats. Her sessions aim to build awareness of manipulative connections, such as romance scams, from how they begin to the natural progression they often take. "Introduction, then repeated contact, favors, sensitive requests — the secrecy, the pressure," she says.
Bad actors may tap into any information you post online to find an interest that can be mirrored and exploited, or an acquaintance who can be infiltrated and make an introduction. If someone you know and trust makes an introduction, you might be less likely to "go do due diligence" on the new person, even if they're a stranger, Delaney says.
One of Vaillance's services includes building a "targeting package" around an executive or C-Suite member, says Delaney. "We can show how they are vulnerable and how we would target that organization just by leveraging the people around them in that circle: spouses, friends, kids, parents, administrative assistants, neighbors," she says. "That's when people's eyes open."
From there, she discusses red flags to spot. Conversations that begin with flattery and seemingly innocuous small talk can gradually shift toward digging for information, introductions to colleagues or access to documents, says Delaney. It's human nature to want to be helpful and fulfill friendly requests, she adds. Add a potential romantic connection to the mix, especially amid an ongoing "loneliness epidemic," and the urge to comply can be even harder to resist, she says.
If you feel yourself getting cornered in a situation where a recent acquaintance or romantic partner keeps asking for information you're not comfortable revealing, Delaney says it helps to have first practiced polite refusal. "One of my favorites is: They could just respond with: 'Why do you ask?'" she says. "Put the other person on the defensive. You could give a nondescript answer. You can say you don't know. You can say you can't respond."
If you're ever suspicious of a new connection — even if you don't want to be — do yourself a favor and conduct some basic vetting, she recommends. You might examine their social media profiles and other publicly available information, for example, to see if their story checks out.
If you can't find enough information to allay your suspicions, don't be shy about alerting your employer's security or human resources team, she says. For smaller companies, or scams outside the workplace, you can file a complaint for cyber threats or romance scams with the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Internet Crime Complaint Center.
And pay attention if your new paramour starts asking you specific questions about your finances or work credentials, says Delaney.
"If you have no game at home, and you get off an airplane somewhere and suddenly everyone's all over you, we call that a red flag," she says.

articles.title: Many people ignore these ‘early red flags’ in romance scams, says Harvard-trained psychologist
articles.text:
Most people want a romantic relationship that makes them feel seen, understood and accepted. Romance scammers exploit that desire, trying to manufacture a bond quickly so they can gain access to money or sensitive information.
As a clinical psychologist who has worked with couples and individuals for over a decade, I've seen some of the smartest people be deceived by well-honed tactics designed to lower their defenses.
Genuine intimacy is built slowly through consistent action, shared experiences and a willingness to be flawed and vulnerable. Scammers, on the other hand, rely on urgency, the performance of vulnerability and emotional shortcuts to get what they want.
Here are five signs you might be dealing with a scammer, and how to spot the difference between a real connection and calculated manipulation.
1. Their emotions don't match the weight of what they're sharing
A common sign of emotional manipulation is a mismatch between the content of what someone says and their emotional delivery. To create a false sense of instant intimacy, scammers might prematurely disclose something deeply traumatic. Pay close attention to how they share it.
When someone genuinely opens up about something painful or challenging in their life, it usually coincides with some natural hesitation, vulnerability or awkwardness. With a scammer, the emotion might feel like an artificial layer they pasted onto a rehearsed script. They might appear way too comfortable, polished or even at ease when delivering such personal stories to someone they barely know.
You may be watching a performance designed to make you drop your guard and reciprocate. Because the disclosure is so heavy, many people feel guilty when doubt creeps in, so they will silence their concerns. But if something strikes you as inauthentic, listen to your gut.
2. They escalate the relationship at warp speed
A real connection requires time for a person to earn your trust and a place in your life. Manipulators, on the other hand, often push for exclusivity with urgency. They are quick to use labels like "soulmates" and employ tactics like future-faking — for example, talking about trips, moving in or having children together — within days or weeks.
This isn't someone who is swept up in passion. It's a strategic tactic used to bypass your critical thinking skills. They flood you with an emotional buffet of everything you've been starving for, through constant attention, intense communication, flattery and early grand declarations.
Through these actions, they induce an intense emotional high that makes you overlook inconsistencies, red flags or warning signs. If someone claims you're the love of their life before they even know what you're like on a bad day, they're much more likely to be operating from their own agenda.
3. Their life is an endless string of convenient crises
Every relationship has its share of unexpected stressors, but with a manipulator, drama and emergencies are a core feature of their ploy. Specifically, the crises are always happening just out of your sight, so you can't necessarily verify them.
For example, their lack of consistency might be explained away by a last-minute canceled flight, a problem with their bank or a family emergency that requires immediate help.
Don't get sucked into these crises. Instead, focus on the pattern of the process. Each crisis conveniently prevents you from either meeting other people in their life, verifying their story or seeing them in normal, unscripted settings.
More importantly, they condition you to step into a rescuer role. They are trying to normalize your willingness to devote money and time to keep them afloat as some test of your loyalty and commitment to the relationship.
4. You have no access to their real relationships and routines
Healthy partners who want to create a genuine and lasting connection will want to bring you into their world. Over time, they'll introduce you to their family, friends, co-workers, gym routine, etc. Their ecosystem will feel full, and they'll take concrete steps to integrate you into it.
When someone is running a scam, their entire life feels just out of reach, almost like it's operating in a vacuum. They might keep you far away from the people who actually know them, offer vague or changing details about their work and background, or insist that you keep your relationship private.
Somehow they'll weaponize this privacy as a way of protecting the relationship and keeping what you have special. Secrecy is often the glue that keeps manipulation schemes together. If you can't see how they exist and operate in the world outside of their relationship with you, you're only seeing a curated aspect of them.
5. Your intuition can sense something is off, even when everything looks great on paper
When someone sweeps you off your feet, is attentive and tells you everything you want to hear, it's easy to talk yourself out of what you know in your gut. Many people ignore early red flags because they don't want to seem cynical, paranoid or ungrateful. They want to believe in the love and connection that's being fostered.
Authentic relationships make you feel safe, calm and increasingly clear-headed over time. Manipulators will often leave you feeling anxious, confused and rushed. If you find yourself constantly rationalizing their behavior or explaining contradictions in their stories, pay attention.
Ultimately, the best way to protect yourself from being scammed is to refuse to skip the foundational steps that real trust is built on. In new relationships, slow down the pace, verify their lofty words with consistent action, and pay attention to whether their vulnerability feels lived-in or rehearsed. Genuine connection never requires you to abandon your basic gut instincts to prove your devotion.
Sabrina Romanoff is a Harvard-trained clinical psychologist, professor, and writer specializing in relationships, high-achievement, and anxiety, with a private practice in New York City. She has been featured in The New York Times, Forbes, Women's Health, USA Today, and on CBS and ABC. Follow her on Instagram @DrSabrinaRomanoff.

articles.title: Hassett denies report he's leaving White House: 'Not true'
articles.text:
National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett on Friday poured cold water on a report that he's expected to leave the White House in the coming weeks.
That report is "not true," Hassett told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a text message.
Semafor reported earlier Friday afternoon that Hassett "has been inquiring about roles outside the administration," even before Republicans' drubbing in last week's midterm election.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and his counselor David Zervos, are among the names being floated to replace Hassett, according to Semafor, which cited unnamed people familiar with his plans.
But a White House official told CNBC in a statement later Friday, "There is no factual basis for this reporting."
"Kevin Hassett is a key member of President Trump's economic team and will continue working to advance President Trump's economic policies," the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the matter.
Zervos, reached by phone after Semafor's story published, declined to comment.
While Hassett denies he is departing the White House, several other Trump administration officials have stepped down since Democrats' staggering wins in the Nov. 3 midterm, flipping Congress blue and overhauling President Donald Trump's plans for the rest of his term.
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles left her role Friday and was succeeded by Stephen Miller. Multiple Department of Justice officials have also left since Election Day, including Harmeet Dhillon, a leader in the DOJ's civil rights division, and John Eisenberg, who headed the national security division.

articles.title: Next week brings 2 big tests of the AI trade, and a handful of portfolio earnings
articles.text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. Stocks fell on Friday for two key reasons . The AI theme came under pressure over concerns that Nvidia's next leader may be less willing to support the broader artificial intelligence ecosystem through financial backstops and investments. These "circular deals" were already being questioned by many, including us, over whether they were necessary, and those concerns had put a cap on Nvidia's valuation. Despite a volatile week, the AI buildout theme had a positive week, recovering some of last week's sharp losses. The other headwind was the continued rise in market interest rates. The 10-year Treasury yield settled last Friday at 4.86%. It's on track to finish this week at around 5.15%, which would be an increase of roughly 29 basis points. That's a pretty big move. Rates surged in response to a couple of hot inflation readings that significantly increased expectations for multiple rate hikes over the next three Federal Reserve meetings. A sustained decline in oil could make some of these calls for tighter monetary policy look too hawkish, but the direction of energy prices will largely depend on what happens next in the Middle East conflict. Higher rates are a drag on companies that need to borrow to grow, which would make financing the AI buildout that much more challenging, especially without Nvidia's financial backing. Given the uncertainties that lie ahead for the AI buildout and interest rates, we remained mostly cash neutral for the week, partially offsetting purchases of Corona and Modelo brewer Constellation Brands and consumer products powerhouse Kimberly-Clark , which diversify the portfolio with low-multiple, less cyclical, dividend-paying companies, through sales of industrial data center play Eaton, diversified healthcare company Cardinal Health , and off-price retailer TJX Companies . There are two key AI events next week . Club name Nvidia reports quarterly earnings without Jensen Huang for the first time, following the co-founder's resignation as CEO and from the board on Thursday amid an affair scandal. In prior quarters, Huang used the earnings calls to share his predictions of AI spending. No one had a better sense than Huang of where the AI puck was heading next. In his absence, interim CEO and long-time CFO Colette Kress is a steady hand who will keep the company on its AI roadmap. We also suspect Kress will share her thoughts on whether the company will continue to invest and backstop other companies and projects in its ecosystem to support the buildout. Finally, we expect to hear more about the company's sales exposure to the Asia Pacific region, and what the future could look like under tighter U.S. export controls. The other major AI event next week is Anthropic's IPO. The frontier AI lab is expected to price its upcoming IPO in a range of $70 and $78 per share, raising tens of billions of dollars for the company. A successful offering could improve sentiment around the broader AI trade. Anthropic is expected to begin trading this coming Thursday. Three other portfolio names report earnings next week. We'll get quarterly reports from Home Depot and TJX. We cut our TJX position in half on Friday over concerns that competitive pressures and internal execution miscues will plague T.J. Maxx and Marshalls' sales for the second quarter in a row. Palo Alto Networks also reports earnings next week. We expect that the firm is performing well given the fact that corporations of all sizes need to strengthen their cybersecurity solutions to protect against AI threats. Analysts at KeyBanc on Friday used the recent pullback in Palo Alto to upgrade their rating to buy from hold. Other earnings and economic numbers next week include Disney, Target, Lowe's, Walmart, Alibaba, Bath & Body Works, Gap, and Ross Stores, and Elastic, as well as data on retail sales, industrial production, housing starts and building permits, pending home sales, and the University of Michigan survey of consumer sentiment and inflation expectations. Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. If Jim has talked about a stock on CNBC TV, he waits 72 hours after issuing the trade alert before executing the trade. articles.title: Nvidia turmoil reshuffles the AI trade. Winners, losers and what investors should watch
articles.text: Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia is scrambling the tech landscape as investors try to gauge the fallout for chip makers, neoclouds, and others in the artificial intelligence arms race. The market has quickly passed judgement — bidding up shares of chipmakers like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom while pushing down neoclouds such as Coreweave and AI server maker Dell Technologies . Traders can benefit from the volatility, but the market has a tendency to overshoot in both directions and estimates are changing rapidly. Long-term investors may want to wait until the dust settles. The market's initial take is that Nvidia's rivals have an opening to capture chip sales while Nvidia undergoes a leadership transition and conducts an internal investigation of Huang's activities. Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday, Nov. 17, and is expected to provide updates under interim CEO Colette Kress. AMD and Broadcom are both up around 17% over the past week, even after a pullback on Friday. The companies are expected to benefit from the turmoil at Nvidia, potentially grabbing market share for GPUs, in AMD's case, and custom AI chips, for Broadcom. "The biggest thing that Nvidia now has to try to reestablish is trust. Once you lose the customer's trust, it is going to benefit competitors," said Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets. "Given the cloud over Nvidia, this is the time for them to capitalize on the trust factor," he added. AMD leads the pack AMD is Wall Street's clearest winner if Nvidia customers shift some AI chip orders to other suppliers. The company competes with Nvidia in core GPUs — chips that handle AI core compute tasks like inference and training large models. "If Nvidia stumbles as a result of internal chaos, we see AMD as the clearest likely beneficiary," Wedbush analyst Matthew Bryson said in a Thursday note, citing a massive need for AI GPUs beyond Nvidia. He reiterated a buy on the stock and $600 target. William Blair analyst Sebastien Naji also recommends AMD, saying the company has made "significant progress" in its Helios racks and secured large commitments for chips from OpenAI, Meta Platforms and Anthropic. Naji has a buy on the stock but no price target. Freedom Capital Market's Woods highlights AMD's technical strength, noting that the chip maker held up well during the recent chip selloff around the midterms. "It held it like a champ, then it rallied, and now it's closer to new highs than any of its competitors in the index," Woods said. That doesn't mean it's all clear for AMD. Pricing pressure is a worry if the U.S. cracks down on chip sales to China, notes Northland Capital Markets analyst Gus Richard. Tougher restrictions on chip exports to China could hit roughly 11% of GPU demand, compelling Nvidia to unload inventory and putting downward pressure on prices for AI GPUs. AMD may already be seeing a slowdown. Its inventory days — a measure of how long it holds chips before selling them — were up quarter over quarter at the end of October, Richard notes. More upside in AMD depends on whether it can grab market share from Nvidia, while maintaining pricing. A domestic slowdown in data center construction or more restrictions on China chip sales remain key risks. Still, AMD's average price target is $657, implying 23% gains from recent prices around $532. Earnings estimates for 2027 are up to $17.75 a share from $16.28 on October 30. Custom chips could win Broadcom and Alphabet stand to gain if more companies turn to chips built for specific AI workloads. Wedbush's Bryson sees an opening for Broadcom's custom application-specific integrated circuits or ASICs. "Custom ASICs are where we believe companies want to turn," he said in a note. For example, Meta has a long-term partnership with Broadcom to help build Meta Platforms ' custom MTIA chip. Elsewhere, Nvidia chip alternatives like Alphabet's tensor processing units (TPUs) "can win at scale" according to William Blair's Naji. Broadcom also helps develop and manufacture Google's TPUs, though Google is diversifying from Broadcom. Despite some big gains lately, Broadcom stock is roughly flat for the year. Analysts see roughly 50% upside from recent prices around $345 with an average target of $526. While Broadcom could benefit from a shift from Nvidia, it's also facing pressures. Rothschild & Co. analyst Mike Harrison downgraded the stock to neutral on Friday, with a $398.47 target. Among his concerns: Broadcom's reliance on OpenAI and Anthropic, tighter AI financing, and Google's move to design more chips in-house. "Google's efforts to diversify away from Broadcom represent an important analogue for gauging the durability of Broadcom's revenues from Anthropic and OpenAI," he wrote. "If Google's strategy works well, the market is likely to assume frontier labs eventually follow suit." Arista could gain from networking shift A shift from Nvidia infrastructure to custom accelerators — chips designed to speed up certain AI workloads — should benefit cloud networking provider, Arista Networks , according to Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani. Arista, which sells high-speed Ethernet switches and routing platforms for data centers, is the "clearest beneficiary" in that area, he wrote. A less dominant Nvidia "could accelerate adoption of open Ethernet architectures versus Nvidia's more vertically integrated networking stack," he wrote in a note on Thursday. Arista's stock is up 54% this year but 2027 earnings estimates keep rising, including a jump from $5.25 to $6.05 a share since October 30, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Daryanani has a buy on the stock and $250 target, implying 26% gains from recent trading around $197. CoreWeave and Dell face rising pressure On the other side of the trade, neoclouds like CoreWeave may be under more stress if Nvidia pulls back on chip financing. Nvidia is both a chip supplier and financial backer of the neocloud, which is building and equipping data centers with plans to rent out massive amounts of AI compute. "All GPUs deployed across CoreWeave's infrastructure today are Nvidia, while the company has also benefited from Nvidia investment and broader strategic partnership/capacity agreements," wrote Daryanani. Brokerages like Goldman Sachs are standing by Coreweave, but others are skeptical. Despite a steep slide in CoreWeave stock, Bernstein analysts still view it as "under punished," according to a note on Friday. The decline "is directionally appropriate given its more direct exposure to AI cloud spending and capacity-delivery risk," Bernstein analysts wrote. While its forward multiple has compressed 61%, they see room for another roughly 10% decline. The problem for Dell, Daryanani noted, is that a majority of its AI server revenues come from Nvidia systems. "Dell would also face some risk given the size of its NVIDIA-based AI server business" as the company targets fiscal 2027 AI server revenues of roughly $74 billion, he noted. Dell slumped 7% Friday amid rising concerns about its growth. The stock is still up 173% this year, however. Wall Street's average target is $595, 72% higher than recent trading around $344.

articles.title: A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process
articles.text:
Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.
However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.
Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options. Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.
This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.
This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.
The trade:
- Buy 100 shares Nvidia
- Sell 1 Dec 18 $185 call
By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

articles.title: Nvidia hasn’t selected search firm for permanent Huang replacement, board tells CNBC
articles.text:
Nvidia hasn't yet selected a search firm to work with in identifying a successor for former CEO Jensen Huang, the company's board told CNBC.
"We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role," the board said in a Friday statement. "We have not formally engaged any potential candidates."
The comments come after speculation has swirled about who might be tapped to replace Huang. Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang would step down as CEO of the chipmaker after multiple reported affairs, including one with a woman purported to be a Chinese spy.
Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO and said it will begin a search for a permanent CEO to replace Huang, adding that it will consider both internal and external candidates. Kress conducted her first meeting as interim CEO on Thursday afternoon with high-level executives at Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif., according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named in order to discuss internal details.
The Financial Times reported Friday that Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas in its search for Huang's successor, citing people familiar with the matter.
Nvidia's board said, "Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature."
Before joining the SoftBank-backed chip company in 2013, Haas spent seven years at Nvidia, serving in a variety of roles including vice president of its computing products business.
Nvidia shares fell more than 2% on Friday, dragging the company's market cap below $4 trillion as investors digested the news of Huang's departure, and the specter of ongoing probes into his conduct.
On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Wachtell Lipton to investigate allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, following revelations that its then-CEO had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang, who several outlets reported is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence.
Three House committees have asked Huang to appear for briefings, and renewed those calls even after the CEO's resignation. The Senate Banking Committee has also requested that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify to discuss "serious concerns about our national security," and how the company's top AI chips have reportedly ended up in China.

articles.title: Chính phủ cho phép EVN dùng lợi nhuận xử lý chi phí đầu tư thất bại
articles.text:
Chính phủ cho phép EVN dùng lợi nhuận xử lý chi phí đầu tư thất bại
Chi phí đầu tư tại các dự án điện không thể triển khai do thay đổi quy hoạch, chính sách được xử lý từ lợi nhuận sau thuế của Tập đoàn Điện lực Việt Nam khi đáp ứng các điều kiện theo quy định. Thời gian phân bổ tối đa là 5 năm.
- 13-11-2026Việt Nam đang đào sâu xuống lòng đất 500m, xây dựng công trình 21.000 tỷ đồng, lớn nhất Đông Nam Á
Cơ chế xử lý chi phí đầu tư thất bại
Chính phủ vừa ban hành Nghị định 407/2026 quy định cơ chế hoạt động, cơ chế quản lý tài chính đặc thù đối với Công ty mẹ - Tập đoàn Điện lực Việt Nam (EVN).
Một nội dung đáng chú ý của nghị định là cơ chế xử lý chi phí đầu tư thất bại tại các dự án, công trình điện lực có tính đặc thù, rủi ro cao. Đây là những khoản chi không được trừ khi xác định thu nhập chịu thuế theo pháp luật về thuế thu nhập doanh nghiệp, được xử lý từ nguồn lợi nhuận sau thuế.
Các khoản chi này bao gồm chi phí chuẩn bị đầu tư và chi phí đầu tư đã thực hiện theo quy định của pháp luật, thuộc hai trường hợp cụ thể.
Thứ nhất, dự án, công trình điện lực không đủ điều kiện triển khai do cơ quan nhà nước có thẩm quyền điều chỉnh quy hoạch.
Thứ hai, dự án, công trình không đủ điều kiện triển khai do cơ quan nhà nước có thẩm quyền ban hành hoặc sửa đổi chính sách, làm thay đổi điều kiện đầu tư. Việc thay đổi chính sách phải là nguyên nhân trực tiếp, quyết định dẫn đến dự án không còn đủ điều kiện triển khai.
Nghị định quy định hồ sơ xác định chi phí đầu tư thất bại phải có các văn bản, báo cáo đánh giá ảnh hưởng của việc điều chỉnh quy hoạch hoặc thay đổi chính sách; hồ sơ nghiệm thu, thanh quyết toán và báo cáo kiểm toán độc lập tương ứng với từng trường hợp.
Căn cứ báo cáo kiểm toán chấp nhận toàn phần của kiểm toán độc lập về giá trị thanh quyết toán, EVN quyết định thời gian phân bổ tối đa 5 năm, kể từ khi Hội đồng thành viên phê duyệt đủ điều kiện quyết toán.
Cho phép phân bổ một số khoản chi qua nhiều năm
Về doanh thu và chi phí, chênh lệch tỷ giá trong quá trình đầu tư các công trình điện lực nằm trong Quy hoạch phát triển điện lực quốc gia được phản ánh lũy kế, phân bổ vào doanh thu hoặc chi phí tài chính. Thời gian phân bổ chi phí không quá 5 năm kể từ khi công trình đi vào hoạt động. Riêng dự án quan trọng quốc gia, thời gian phân bổ không quá thời gian trả nợ khoản vay.
Chi phí công tơ điện cũng được phân bổ trong thời gian không quá 5 năm kể từ thời điểm phát sinh, phù hợp với tình hình sản xuất kinh doanh của EVN.
Đối với chi phí sửa chữa, khắc phục sự cố công trình điện lực do nguyên nhân khách quan như thiên tai, hỏa hoạn, EVN được phân bổ không quá 3 năm kể từ thời điểm phát sinh nếu khoản chi làm giảm lãi so với kế hoạch hoặc gây lỗ. Phần được phân bổ là chi phí còn lại sau khi trừ tiền bồi thường bảo hiểm và các nguồn hỗ trợ khác, nếu có.
Về quản lý tài sản, Hội đồng thành viên EVN được quyết định chuyển giao dự án đầu tư, tài sản, công trình điện lực giữa EVN và các công ty con do tập đoàn nắm giữ 100% vốn điều lệ. Việc chuyển giao thực hiện nguyên trạng theo giá trị sổ sách, không đánh giá lại giá trị; ghi tăng, giảm vốn theo quy định.
Với công trình điện lực đầu tư theo phương thức đối tác công tư mà EVN nhận chuyển giao, trường hợp không có thông tin về nguyên giá và giá trị còn lại của tài sản, giá trị công trình được tạm xác định bằng 20% giá trị vốn đầu tư công trình điện. Sau đó, EVN tiếp tục thực hiện các bước xác định giá trị theo quy định.
Các công trình thuộc diện này đã được EVN nhận chuyển giao trước ngày nghị định có hiệu lực nhưng chưa hoàn thành xác định giá trị để tạm ghi tăng tài sản, tăng vốn đầu tư của chủ sở hữu cũng được áp dụng cơ chế tạm ghi giá trị tài sản từ thời điểm nhận bàn giao.
Tiền phong

articles.title: Supreme Court agrees to hear Robinhood challenge to IPO information omission lawsuit
articles.text:
The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to hear a case in which Robinhood seeks to block a class-action lawsuit over the omission of interim financial data from the online broker's initial public offering in 2021.
Robinhood wants the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling by the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals that revived a lawsuit by investors against the company and firms involved with the IPO, including Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan Securities.
A San Francisco federal court judge had previously dismissed the lawsuit.
The Trump administration and the Securities and Exchange Commission had urged the Supreme Court to hear Robinhood's appeal.
"We are pleased the Supreme Court has agreed to hear our case and look forward to presenting our argument," a Robinhood spokesperson said in a statement.
CNBC has requested comment from the attorneys representing the plaintiffs in the case.
Robinhood's IPO came on the heels of a surge in investor interest during the Covid-19 pandemic in so-called meme stocks, and trading in the crypto asset dogecoin.
In July 2021, Robinhood conducted its IPO, "for which it prepared a registration statement" that "contained only limited information about Robinhood's performance during the second quarter of 2021," the 9th Circuit panel that heard the case noted.
"After the initial public offering, Robinhood reported financial results from that second quarter, and its stock price dropped," the panel wrote.
The investors who sued Robinhood and the other defendants alleged the registration statement omitted material information it was legally required to disclose.

articles.title: Đóng bảo hiểm trực tuyến đã bị trừ tiền nhưng chưa ghi nhận, người dân cần làm gì?
articles.text:
Đóng bảo hiểm trực tuyến đã bị trừ tiền nhưng chưa ghi nhận, người dân cần làm gì?
Người dân đã bị trừ tiền khi đóng bảo hiểm xã hội tự nguyện, gia hạn thẻ bảo hiểm y tế trực tuyến nhưng hệ thống chưa ghi nhận kết quả cần liên hệ đơn vị cung cấp dịch vụ thanh toán và cơ quan bảo hiểm xã hội để tra soát, không tự ý thanh toán lại nhằm tránh phát sinh giao dịch trùng lặp.
- 13-11-2026Tất cả người dân có lương hưu, trợ cấp trên cả nước chú ý thông tin quan trọng về kỳ lương tháng 12
- 13-11-2026Từ năm 2026, một nhóm người nghỉ hưu có thể nhận thêm 50 triệu đồng, thậm chí nhiều hơn ngoài lương hưu
- 12-11-2026Chính phủ vừa phê duyệt chính sách quan trọng liên quan đến một nhóm trẻ em Việt Nam: Đặt mục tiêu 100% trường hợp đủ điều kiện được hưởng 2 quyền lợi đặc biệt
Ngày 14-11, Bảo hiểm xã hội (BHXH) Việt Nam cho biết, qua rà soát, cơ quan này ghi nhận một số trường hợp người dân đã thanh toán qua các ứng dụng MoMo, VNPAY, MB Bank để gia hạn thẻ bảo hiểm y tế (BHYT) hoặc đóng tiếp BHXH tự nguyện, nhưng hệ thống BHXH chưa nhận được thông tin hoặc khoản tiền nên chưa ghi nhận kết quả giao dịch.
Một số trường hợp khác, tiền đã vào tài khoản thu của cơ quan BHXH nhưng thông tin ngân hàng chuyển đến chưa đầy đủ hoặc không đúng định dạng, khiến hệ thống không thể tự động hạch toán, cập nhật quá trình tham gia. Những trường hợp này phải được cán bộ BHXH tra soát, xử lý thủ công.
Ngoài ra, một số giao dịch không thành công do chưa đáp ứng điều kiện nghiệp vụ. Khi gia hạn thẻ BHYT, người tham gia có thể gặp lỗi do thông tin đăng ký cơ sở khám chữa bệnh ban đầu không phù hợp, cơ sở đã ngừng hoạt động, không tiếp nhận đăng ký khám chữa bệnh ngoại tỉnh hoặc thời hạn thẻ bị trùng.
Đối với việc đóng tiếp BHXH tự nguyện, nguyên nhân có thể do số tiền đóng không đủ, giao dịch đã phát sinh trước đó hoặc người tham gia đang đóng BHXH tại đơn vị khác.
Trong tháng 10-2026, phần mềm thu và quản lý sổ, thẻ của BHXH Việt Nam tiếp nhận 12.664 giao dịch gia hạn thẻ BHYT hộ gia đình và đóng tiếp BHXH tự nguyện. Trong đó, 12.250 giao dịch thành công, 414 giao dịch không thành công.
BHXH Việt Nam khuyến nghị, sau khi thanh toán, người dân cần kiểm tra trạng thái giao dịch, thông tin thanh toán và kết quả ghi nhận trên hệ thống. Với thẻ BHYT, cần kiểm tra kết quả gia hạn và thời hạn sử dụng; với BHXH tự nguyện, cần xác nhận khoản đóng đã được ghi nhận hay chưa.
Trường hợp tài khoản đã bị trừ tiền nhưng hệ thống chưa cập nhật, người tham gia cần liên hệ đơn vị cung cấp dịch vụ thanh toán và cơ quan BHXH để được kiểm tra, tra soát. Người dân nên lưu chứng từ, mã giao dịch, thời điểm và số tiền thanh toán để thuận tiện đối chiếu; không tự ý thanh toán lại khi chưa xác định rõ trạng thái giao dịch trước đó, tránh phát sinh khoản đóng trùng.
Để hạn chế vướng mắc, BHXH Việt Nam khuyến nghị người dân thực hiện giao dịch qua Cổng Dịch vụ công quốc gia hoặc các ngân hàng đã ký thỏa thuận phối hợp thu với cơ quan BHXH, gồm BIDV, Vietcombank, Agribank và VietinBank. Cổng Dịch vụ công BHXH Việt Nam hiện đang được điều chỉnh, nâng cấp.
BHXH Việt Nam cũng đề nghị BHXH các tỉnh, thành phố thường xuyên rà soát, đối chiếu những khoản tiền đã nhận nhưng chưa được hệ thống ghi nhận; kịp thời kiểm tra, cập nhật dữ liệu đóng BHXH, BHYT, bảo đảm quyền lợi người tham gia.
Sài Gòn Giải Phóng

articles.title: Retirees sometimes tap savings for one-off expenses. Here’s what advisors say to consider first
articles.text:
Retirees facing a large expense that's not in their regular household budget may turn to their traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account balances to cover it.
While retirement savings may be the easiest place to turn for the money, financial advisors say there are a few things worth considering before making one-off withdrawals.
"Be aware of the fact that it's not as simple as just taking out the amount of money that [covers] what you want it for," said certified financial planner Victoria Trumbower, managing member of Trumbower Financial Advisors in Bethesda, Maryland. The firm ranked No. 19 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026.
At the same time, research shows that many retirees aren't even spending their nest egg. About a third still have 100% or more of their initial assets when they reach their mid-80s, according to a May study by the Employee Benefit Research Institute, a nonpartisan research group.
"Retirement savings are meant to be spent," said CFP Alex Canellopoulos, director of wealth and a partner with Vista Capital Partners in Portland, Oregon. "A one-time withdrawal isn't necessarily a bad decision, as long as it fits within a sustainable retirement plan."
Unplanned withdrawals often go toward debt
In 2025, about 15% of 401(k) owners ages 60 to 72 with balances of at least $100,000 who had left their employer made an ad hoc withdrawal from their account, according to Vanguard's How America Retires 2026 report, which analyzed more than 125,000 ex-plan participants.
This age group falls between the onset of penalty-free withdrawals — age 59½ — and the threshold for starting required minimum distributions — currently age 73. RMDs are amounts that retirees must withdraw annually from traditional 401(k)s and IRAs.
Not all 401(k) plans allow occasional withdrawals from ex-employees — about 43% did in 2025, up from 16% in 2015, the Vanguard study says. If a plan doesn't offer such ad hoc distributions, a former employee who wants to tap that money would have to withdraw or roll over the entire balance. Typically, they roll it over to an IRA and take withdrawals from there.
The most common reasons for retirees taking irregular distributions, based on a 2025 Vanguard survey of 8,000 clients noted in the recent report, are paying off debt, with 31% of respondents citing it; covering unforeseen expenses such as medical care and home repairs, noted by 23%; and discretionary spending, with 22% citing it as a reason.
Don't overlook the tax hit
Regardless of why you take the money, advisors say a key consideration is the impact on your tax situation.
Distributions from a traditional 401(k) or IRA are generally taxed as ordinary income. If you don't have other means to cover the tax bill, you may have to withdraw extra from your retirement account to compensate — which creates a tricky situation.
"It's like a double whammy because you have to pay income tax, but you don't have any money to pay income tax, so you've got to withdraw more money to pay the tax, and then you've got to pay taxes" on the extra amount, Trumbower said.
It's going to cost you a lot more than you think.Victoria TrumbowerManaging member of Trumbower Financial Advisors
For illustration: If you need $50,000 after taxes and assume a combined federal and state income tax rate of 25%, the math says you would need to withdraw about $66,667. That's because the money withdrawn to cover the tax bill is itself taxable. A $66,667 withdrawal taxed at 25% would result in about $16,667 in taxes, leaving $50,000 after tax.
"It's going to cost you a lot more than you think," Trumbower said.
There may be an undesirable ripple effect
A taxable withdrawal from retirement savings can also trigger additional costs elsewhere.
For example, if you're receiving Social Security retirement benefits, the added income could cause a larger portion of that money to become taxable. Depending on how much other income you have, 0%, up to 50%, or up to 85% of your Social Security benefits may be subject to federal income tax. A large retirement-account withdrawal can increase that other income and make more of your benefits taxable.
For retirees on Medicare, a large taxable withdrawal also could increase their Part B and Part D premiums through the income-related monthly adjustment amount, or IRMAA.
For 2026, that surcharge applies when modified adjusted gross income exceeds $109,000 for an individual filer or $218,000 for a married couple filing jointly. Medicare generally bases the surcharge on tax information from two years earlier, meaning 2026 premiums are typically based on 2024 income.
"What catches many people off guard is that they often don't feel that impact until a couple of years after the withdrawal," said CFP Ciano Villaquiran, a partner with CURO Financial Planning in San Diego.
Consider delaying part of the withdrawal
For some retirees, it may be worth delaying the additional withdrawal needed to cover the tax bill until the next calendar year, Trumbower said. That second distribution would be taxable in the following year, potentially spreading the income — and its tax impact — across two tax years.
"Pushing the [additional] distribution from the IRA into the following calendar year may possibly avoid jumping up into a higher tax bracket," Trumbower said.
However, she said, retirees should still withhold enough tax from the initial distribution to avoid an underpayment penalty. The federal income tax system is generally pay-as-you-go, meaning taxpayers must pay enough tax through withholding or estimated payments during the year rather than waiting until they file their return.
Generally, taxpayers can avoid an underpayment penalty if their withholding and estimated payments equal at least 90% of the current year's tax liability or 100% of the prior year's tax liability. For certain higher-income taxpayers, the prior-year threshold is 110%. Any remaining tax due generally can be paid when the return is filed.
Other ways to cover the expense
If you have a brokerage account, that may be a better source to fund a one-off expense, Trumbower said.
Taxes on long-term capital gains — profits on investments such as stocks held for more than one year — are generally lower than ordinary income tax rates. Depending on your taxable income, some long-term capital gains may even be taxed at 0%.
For 2026, the 0% long-term capital gains rate applies to taxable income of up to $49,450 for single filers and $98,900 for married couples filing jointly. Above those thresholds, most long-term capital gains are taxed at 15%, with a 20% rate applying at higher income levels.
Weigh the pros and cons of borrowing the money
Depending on the expense, retirees may be able to borrow money instead of tapping their savings, Trumbower said.
For example, a home equity loan or line of credit could help pay for a major home improvement project, while a car purchase could be financed with an auto loan rather than a large withdrawal from retirement savings.
Of course, borrowing comes with its own costs and risks. The loan payments would need to fit within the retiree's budget, and the interest paid could outweigh the potential benefits of leaving retirement savings untouched.
The withdrawal could have long-term repercussions
Additionally, it's worth considering how the withdrawal could affect your savings over time.
"Pulling a large amount out for a one-time expense doesn't just reduce the account balance today; it can reduce what that money could have grown into down the road," Villaquiran said.
For illustration: $50,000 earning 5% annually would grow to about $81,400 after 10 years, according to the Securities and Exchange Commission's Investor.gov compound-interest calculator. If a retiree withdrew $10,000 at the start and left $40,000 invested under the same assumptions, it would grow to about $65,200 — a difference of roughly $16,300 after 10 years.
